analysis.one_liner: Lets FDA inspect large animal farms during foodborne-illness outbreak investigations.
analysis.headline: The bill, giving FDA authority to sample livestock operations during outbreak investigations, has sat in the Senate health committee since February 2025 with no action and only two sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When food poisoning outbreaks happen, the FDA currently cannot go onto large animal feeding operations to take samples of animals, water, or the environment to find the source. This bill would let the FDA request access to those operations during an outbreak investigation, with penalties for operations that refuse. Data from sampling would be shared with the Agriculture Department and state and federal health agencies.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who get sick from contaminated meat, poultry, and produce — foodborne illness sends roughly tens of thousands of Americans to the hospital each year — plus state and federal investigators who currently have to work around farms they cannot enter. Speeding up the search for an outbreak's root cause means fewer people eat contaminated food before a recall happens.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers and public health investigators

how_it_helps.text: The FDA may request access to a concentrated animal feeding operation when it determines sampling is necessary for an outbreak investigation, to determine an outbreak's root cause, or to address other public health needs [S2] [S3].

Operations must provide reasonable access for sampling of plants, animals, water, and the environment, and refusing access becomes a prohibited act under the food and drug law, subject to penalties [S2] [S3].
Data collected must be shared with the Secretary of Agriculture and state and federal public health agencies to help detect, investigate, and prevent foodborne illness [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large confined livestock operations, which would have to grant government investigators access to their facilities, animals, and water during outbreaks and could face penalties for refusing. Operators can set reasonable conditions on time, place, and manner of sampling [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill gives federal investigators a legal right to enter private farm property and sample animals, water, and the environment, an intrusion farm groups could resist as heavy-handed, and refusal carries penalties [S3].

The bill expressly does not add requirements beyond microbial sampling for meat, poultry, and egg products, which are regulated by the Department of Agriculture rather than the FDA, so the largest share of outbreak-linked products keeps its existing inspection regime [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster tracing of food poisoning outbreaks to their source on large livestock operations, which protects consumers before recalls or warnings go out. The cost falls on a specific set of large confined animal operations, which must allow access but may set reasonable conditions on how and when sampling happens. A real limit is that the most outbreak-prone products — meat and poultry — sit under USDA jurisdiction, and the bill carves those out beyond sampling, so the reach is narrower than the problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee in February 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Booker (for himself and Senator Blumenthal) on February 3, 2025 [S3] [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on February 3, 2025, which is the only action since [S5].
It has one cosponsor, Senator Blumenthal (D-CT) [S4] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large concentrated livestock operations, which remain outside FDA's investigative reach during outbreak investigations. Consumers gain nothing yet; the proposal has not moved.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill giving FDA sampling authority over large animal feeding operations during outbreak investigations.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; sole cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators have supported the bill; no Republican support is visible in the record, and no one has publicly opposed it or taken a recorded vote on it [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Large concentrated animal feeding operations (industrial livestock)
industries.note: The bill requires these operations to open their facilities, animals, water, and environment to FDA microbial sampling during outbreak investigations, with penalties for refusal — the first time FDA would have that access. Their interest in keeping operations closed to investigators runs against consumers' interest in fast outbreak tracing [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Meat, poultry, and egg products industry
industries.note: The bill explicitly limits FDA to microbial sampling on foods under USDA jurisdiction, adding no new requirements for meat, poultry, or eggs, so the industry's existing inspection regime is largely untouched [S3].

analysis.trajectory: With only two sponsors, no cosponsors from the other party, and no committee action more than a year into the 119th Congress, the bill is following the path of most food-safety measures: it will likely die quietly in the HELP Committee unless a major outbreak or a push from leadership puts it on the agenda.
